newsitem.title: USA: San Francisco sues Bank of America over bonds.
newsitem.headline: San Francisco sues Bank of America over bonds.

text.p: San Francisco on Thursday sued BankAmerica Corp., the nation's third largest bank, alleging it mishandled hundreds of millions of dollars in municipal bond funds and engaged in a massive cover-up.

City Attorney Louise Renne said the lawsuit -- seeking at least $12 million in damages -- alleges the bank, acting as a trustee, mishandled bond funds issued for low-income housing, schools, fire protection and other public works.
San Francisco's 61-page lawsuit alleges that Bank of America lost control on a "massive scale" of hundreds of millions of dollars in bond funds entrusted to the bank.
"The bank has breached the public's trust," Renne said. "The evidence we have of mismanagement and cover-up will shock the harshest critic of the banking industry."
City attorneys, who filed the lawsuit Thursday in Superior Court in San Francisco, said they were intervening in a "whistleblower" complaint filed under seal in April 1995.
The "whistleblower" is Patrick Stull, a former vice president for corporate trust at Bank of America.

BankAmerica said San Francisco's claims were "short on reality." It said its Institutional Trust Department, which it sold in 1995, unintentionally overcharged the city for trust services and retained some funds.
"The bank discovered the overcharge errors on its own and voluntarily refunded over $5 million to its customers," said James Roethe, the bank's general counsel.

The Bank of America trust department acted as trustee for municipal bonds issued by San Francisco and other California municipalities. It handled more than $3 billion of San Francisco municipal bonds from 1985 to 1995, according to San Francisco Deputy City Attorney Don Tickle.
San Francisco said it has been investigating Stull's allegations in cooperation with California's attorney general. The attorney general confirmed that it was conducting a probe.
"The state has been involved in an investigation with Bank of America for several months," the state attorney general's spokesman Rob Stutzman said. He declined further comment.

These investigations have centered on Institutional Trust Department, which Bank of America sold in 1995 to several other banks, including First Trust Bank. San Francisco said it is not suing First Trust.
State sources said California's investigation of Bank of America involves alleged overbilling for trustee services.
Renne said the San Francisco suit could spur other cities and counties in California and other states to take action.
Miguel Dager, Deputy City Attorney for Los Angeles said, "We've been monitoring the situation with San Francisco and the state attorney general.

"I would expect our losses to be in the millions of dollars. I think that our damages could be as much as San Francisco's, depending upon the money that the bank failed to revert back to city," he said.
But Dager said he did not expect Los Angeles to file its own suit individually. "If we are involved in a suit, it will be in conjunction with the attorney general," he said.

BankAmerica said its exposure to San Francisco's claims would be immaterial. Analyst George Salem of Gerard Klauer Mattison said, "From my point of view, it's immaterial and will probably translate into pennies per share in a one-time charge."
The bonds involved in the San Francisco lawsuit were issued by the city, the San Francisco School District, the San Francisco Housing Authority and the San Francisco Redevelopment Agency.

Renne said the city's $12 million estimate of damages could be revised to $17 million or more as the probe continues and that the city could be entitled to three times the actual damages if it prevails in the lawsuit.
The San Francisco suit alleges the bank arbitrarily eliminated the records of bonds, and created false records to show that outstanding bonds had been paid when in fact they had not.
The lawsuit said BankAmerica kept millions of dollars of unclaimed payments of interest on bonds and made unauthorized investments with funds the bank was holding in trust.
Renne said the bank also charged fees for services it did not perform and double charged for services it did perform, and engaged in a "massive cover-up."

Soon after San Francisco launched its investigation of BankAmerica, the bank began to send checks, ranging in size from $100 to $35,000, to city departments in an apparent bid to "put out the fire," deputy city attorney Tickle said.
